doc.title: Joanne Brackeen interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 10, 2001

title: Self-taught: Westlake College, Bird, Bud Powell and transcribing records
summary: With little formal teaching she studied briefly at Westlake College, then found Charlie Parker and Bud Powell and transcribed their solos, a half tone sharp.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Uh huh. So in order to play with these musicians, what kind of preparation did you undergo. Was it — did someone tell you to learn the standards and all that?

It was very weird. They didn’t have really schools that much. There was one school called the Westlake College of Music. And my parents took me there when I was fourteen and I remember studying a little bit with a piano player named Dave Robertson and also one named Gene Garf. And I remember Gene Garf liked Art Tatum a lot and I didn’t at that time. And they would give me a tune a week or something, I would learn a tune, and it would be a standard. They didn’t say anything and it really, there was no way that you learned scales and how to play on things, they just said here’s a tune, you know, improvise on it. So I did. It was kind of hard. But I learned how to do it. I don’t know how I did. And then of course I heard Charlie Parker and that did it for me when I heard that. You know whatever Art Tatum had done for the previous piano teacher, Charlie Parker did that for me. And then of course Bud Powell. So those were my favorites right when I was like seventeen, eighteen. And I used to transcribe the whole thing you know, so I could play it on the record, like a record like that over there, that’s what we had are 33s. And I’d put the record on, transcribe the Bird solo and the Bud solo, so I could play the whole thing. And it would be a half a tone sharp so if it was in the key of F it would

be G flat. But you know the funny thing about not knowing anything too much and not having many teachers was that I didn’t know that was hard, or I didn’t think too much, it was just something I really liked to do. And I thought that the feeling of the music was incredible. I still feel that way when I hear Bird and Bud. Nothing left. So those two are really amazing. A lot of times you hear music, of course I have a different opinion of Art Tatum, I love him now too. But sometimes you know you hear music and it seems to — it changes. It doesn’t but you change and so it sounds changed. But they didn’t.
Do you think Tatum was perhaps too technical for your ears at the time? Or can you think back on that?

I don’t know what it was. I kind of liked the rhythmical feeling of what Bird and Diz and many other people too, Tommy Flanagan was one of the first people I heard, Sonny Rollins, I just thought they were fantastic. I like the rhythmical essence there, and while Art Tatum had it, he would kind of venture off of it and I’m like, now why is he doing that? But then later on, as you get to know the piano better, he is totally amazing. And I love him. And I can listen to him any mood at any time.
Um hum. I like the statement you pointed out just a moment ago though about the not knowing something was supposed to be difficult.
Yes. No, there were no teachers then.
Right. So it didn’t get in your way, that you had to play in the key of G flat.
